title: Assessing Effects of Task and Data Distribution on the Effectiveness of Visual Encodings
authors: Young-Hoon Kim, Jeffrey Heer
venue: Computer Graphics Forum
finding: Across 12 encodings of trivariate data, rankings depend on task and data distribution: colored scatterplots excel at comparing individual points but degrade for summary tasks as the number of categories grows.

title: Modeling Color Difference for Visualization Design
authors: Danielle Albers Szafir
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Perceivable color differences vary significantly by mark type (points, bars, lines); thin or small marks need larger color steps than standard CIELAB distances imply. Provides probabilistic models for sizing color differences.

title: Hypothetical Outcome Plots Help Untrained Observers Judge Trends in Ambiguous Data
authors: Alex M. Kale, Francis Nguyen, Matthew J. Kay et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Animated hypothetical outcome plots (HOPs) let untrained viewers infer the correct underlying trend from weaker evidence than error bars or line ensembles.

title: Face to Face: Evaluating Visual Comparison
authors: Brian Ondov, Nicole L. Jardine, Niklas Elmqvist et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: For visual comparison, overlaid charts beat standard small multiples. Mirror-symmetric small multiples and animated transitions also improved precision, which runs against common design wisdom.

title: The Curse of Knowledge in Visual Data Communication
authors: Cindy Xiong, Lisanne van Weelden, Steven Franconeri
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Curse of knowledge: people who knew a backstory believed naive viewers would see the same pattern as salient, even when told to ignore their knowledge. Presenters systematically overestimate what the audience sees, which argues for stating the takeaway explicitly.

title: Seeing What You Believe or Believing What You See? Belief Biases Correlation Estimation
authors: Cindy Xiong, Chase Stokes, Yea‐Seul Kim et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Correlation estimates were more accurate with generic X/Y labels than with meaningful labels. Strong believers in a relationship overestimated correlation by about r = 0.1.

title: Judgment Error in Pie Chart Variations
authors: Robert Kosara, Drew Skau
venue: EuroVis 2016 (Short Papers)
finding: Every pie variant (exploded, elliptical, square, enlarged slice) produced more error than a regular pie. Shape-distorting variants produced the highest error.

title: Arcs, Angles, or Areas: Individual Data Encodings in Pie and Donut Charts
authors: Drew Skau, Robert Kosara
venue: Computer Graphics Forum
finding: Angle is the least important cue when reading pies and donuts. Donut charts are as accurate as pies.

title: Evidence for Area as the Primary Visual Cue in Pie Charts
authors: Robert Kosara
venue: IEEE VIS 2019 (Short Papers)
finding: In projected 3D pies, area (not angle or arc length) best explains how people read slice values.

title: Beyond Weber's Law: A Second Look at Ranking Visualizations of Correlation
authors: Matthew J. Kay, Jeffrey Heer
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Scatterplots uniquely combine high precision for both positive and negative correlations with low variance between individuals. Weber's-law ranking replaced with a credible partial ranking.

title: Correlation Judgment and Visualization Features: A Comparative Study
authors: Fumeng Yang, Lane Harrison, Ronald A. Rensink et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Of 49 candidate visual features, a small number explain how people judge correlation in scatterplots. Viewers use visual proxies, not statistics.

title: Regression by Eye
authors: Michael Correll, Jeffrey Heer
venue: Proceedings of the 2017 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Viewers estimate trends by eye fairly accurately in standard bivariate charts, but visual and data features (e.g. outliers) cause systematic deviations from least-squares fits.

title: Value-Suppressing Uncertainty Palettes
authors: Michael Correll, Dominik Moritz, Jeffrey Heer
venue: ACM CHI 2018
finding: Value-suppressing uncertainty palettes made people weight uncertainty more heavily in decisions than conventional bivariate color maps.

title: Truncating the Y-Axis: Threat or Menace?
authors: Michael Correll, Enrico Bertini, Steven Franconeri
venue: ACM CHI 2020
finding: Y-axis truncation inflates perceived effect size across chart types (not just bars). Explicit visual cues that the axis is truncated did not remove the bias.

title: Graph Construction
authors: Jessica K. Witt
venue: Meta-Psychology
finding: A y-axis range of about 1.5 SD around the data gave the best sensitivity and lowest bias. Minimal ranges make every effect look big; full 0–100 ranges make every effect look small. Recommendation: at least 1 SD, ideally about 1.5 SD.

title: Truncating bar graphs persistently misleads viewers.
authors: Brenda W. Yang, Camila Vargas Restrepo, Matthew L. Stanley et al.
venue: Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition
finding: 83.5% of participants showed a truncation effect (differences perceived as larger). It persisted after explicit warnings, and graph literacy did not predict susceptibility.

title: Truth or Square: Aspect Ratio Biases Recall of Position Encodings
authors: Cristina R. Ceja, Caitlyn M. McColeman, Cindy Xiong et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Remembered bar values are biased toward a square: wide bars are overestimated and tall bars underestimated. The bias also appears when comparing across sequential views.

title: Rethinking the Ranks of Visual Channels
authors: Caitlyn M. McColeman, Fumeng Yang, Timothy F. Brady et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: When reproducing 2, 4 or 8 values from memory, the classic Cleveland & McGill channel ranking did not hold. Rankings shifted with the number of marks and the error measure.

title: Four types of ensemble coding in data visualizations
authors: Danielle Albers Szafir, Steve Haroz, Michael Gleicher et al.
venue: Journal of Vision
finding: Framework of 4 ensemble-coding tasks (identify, summarize, segment, estimate structure). This underpins the principle that global statistics are extracted fast and subset comparisons are slow.

title: Somewhere Over the Rainbow
authors: Yang Liu, Jeffrey Heer
venue: Proceedings of the 2018 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Colormap performance is best predicted by combining perceptual color-space and color-naming metrics. The rainbow (jet) map performed poorly, while perceptually designed multi-hue maps did better.

title: Rainbows Revisited: Modeling Effective Colormap Design for Graphical Inference
authors: Khairi Reda, Danielle Albers Szafir
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Contrary to guidelines, colormaps that cross many nameable hues (e.g. rainbow) led to more accurate model-based inference than single-hue ramps.

title: Mapping Color to Meaning in Colormap Data Visualizations
authors: Karen B. Schloss, Connor Gramazio, Allison Silverman et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Dark-is-more bias: people assume darker = larger. When a colormap appears to vary in opacity, an opaque-is-more bias takes over, which makes background color matter.

title: Colorgorical: Creating discriminable and preferable color palettes for information visualization
authors: Connor Gramazio, David H. Laidlaw, Karen B. Schloss
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Balancing perceptual distance, name difference and pair preference yields categorical palettes (3, 5 or 8 colors) that are both discriminable and aesthetically preferred.

title: A Survey of Perception-Based Visualization Studies by Task
authors: Ghulam Jilani Quadri, Paul A. Rosen
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Systematic review of perception-based visualization studies since 1980, organized by low-level task, encoding and chart type. Useful as a lookup reference.

title: A Review and Collation of Graphical Perception Knowledge for Visualization Recommendation
authors: Zehua Zeng, Leilani Battle
venue: ACM CHI 2023
finding: Collates 59 graphical-perception papers across 10 analysis tasks into a machine-readable knowledge base and flags inconsistent reporting across studies.

title: The Perceptual Proxies of Visual Comparison
authors: Nicole L. Jardine, Brian Ondov, Niklas Elmqvist et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: The best arrangement depends on the comparison task (biggest mean vs biggest range vs biggest delta). The visual system uses perceptual proxies such as hull area instead of computing true statistics.

title: The Weighted Average Illusion: Biases in Perceived Mean Position in Scatterplots
authors: Matt-Heun Hong, Jessica K. Witt, Danielle Albers Szafir
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Weighted average illusion: larger and darker points pull the perceived mean in bubble or colored scatterplots, and the bias grows with the size or lightness range.

title: Task-Based Effectiveness of Basic Visualizations
authors: Bahador Saket, Alex Endert, Çağatay Demiralp
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Five small chart types (table, line, bar, scatter, pie) across 10 tasks: effectiveness varies strongly by task, with no universal winner. Bar charts were robust across many tasks, while tables and pies did well only on specific ones.

title: Revisiting Channel Effectiveness: A Multi-Dimensional Evaluation with Primitive Visual Stimuli
authors: Soohyun Lee, Seokhyeon Park, Minsuk Chang et al.
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)
finding: Seven channels across 4 perceptual tasks: rankings shift by task. Length gives top accuracy but only moderate pop-out, while area has the highest detection rate but poor accuracy.

title: Evaluating Graphical Perception of Visual Motion for Quantitative Data Encoding
authors: Shaghayegh Esmaeili, Samia Kabir, Anthony Colas et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Motion (especially expansion and translation) can encode quantities competitively with static channels. Non-synchronized motion is read faster and more accurately than synchronized motion.

title: What's the Difference?: Evaluating Variations of Multi-Series Bar Charts for Visual Comparison Tasks
authors: Arjun Srinivasan, Matthew Brehmer, Bongshin Lee et al.
venue: ACM CHI 2018
finding: Among grouped bar charts used in dashboards, adding difference overlays supported a wider range of comparison tasks without hurting single-task performance.

title: Towards Understanding How Readers Integrate Charts and Captions: A Case Study with Line Charts
authors: Dae Hyun Kim, Vidya Setlur, Maneesh Agrawala
venue: ACM CHI 2021
finding: When chart and caption emphasize the same salient feature, it becomes the takeaway. If the caption describes a low-prominence feature, readers ignore it and report the salient chart feature instead.

title: Striking a Balance: Reader Takeaways and Preferences when Integrating Text and Charts
authors: Chase Stokes, Vidya Setlur, Bridget Cogley et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Participants preferred the most heavily annotated charts over sparsely annotated charts and over text alone. The semantic level of the text steers which takeaways people report.

title: Frames and Slants in Titles of Visualizations on Controversial Topics
authors: Ha‐Kyung Kong, Zhicheng Liu, Karrie G. Karahalios
venue: ACM CHI 2018
finding: Slanted titles changed the perceived main message, so viewers took opposite messages from the same chart. There was no significant attitude change.

title: Trust and Recall of Information across Varying Degrees of Title-Visualization Misalignment
authors: Ha‐Kyung Kong, Zhicheng Liu, Karrie G. Karahalios
venue: ACM CHI 2019
finding: Even with contradictory titles, most viewers judged the chart impartial, and recall matched the title more often than the data.

title: Beyond Memorability: Visualization Recognition and Recall
authors: Michelle A. Borkin, Zoya Bylinskii, Nam Wook Kim et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Titles and text draw attention and drive recall. Pictograms do not hurt and can help recognition, and redundancy helps. Charts that are memorable at a glance also convey their message better.

title: Interpreting the Effect of Embellishment on Chart Visualizations
authors: Tiffany Andry, Christophe Hurter, François Lambotte et al.
venue: ACM CHI 2021
finding: Within bounds, embellishments increased engagement with infographics with very limited downside.

title: Learning Visual Importance for Graphic Designs and Data Visualizations
authors: Zoya Bylinskii, Nam Wook Kim, Peter O’Donovan et al.
venue: ACM UIST 2017
finding: Models trained on crowdsourced clicks predict which chart elements people find important (titles, labels, data). Useful for design feedback and thumbnails.

title: BubbleView
authors: Nam Wook Kim, Zoya Bylinskii, Michelle A. Borkin et al.
venue: ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction
finding: Mouse-click 'bubble' reveals approximate eye fixations on visualizations, making attention measurement possible without an eye tracker.

title: Data Visualization Saliency Model: A Tool for Evaluating Abstract Data Visualizations
authors: Laura E. Matzen, Michael Joseph Haass, Kristin Divis et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Classic saliency models predict gaze on charts poorly. A text-aware Data Visualization Saliency model fits eye-tracking data better.

title: Visual Arrangements of Bar Charts Influence Comparisons in Viewer Takeaways
authors: Cindy Xiong, Vidya Setlur, Benjamin Bach et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Bar arrangement (juxtaposed vertically or horizontally, overlaid, stacked) changes which comparisons viewers make. Expert designers' predictions partly mismatched actual viewer takeaways.

title: What Does the Chart Say? Grouping Cues Guide Viewer Comparisons and Conclusions in Bar Charts
authors: Cindy Xiong Bearfield, Chase Stokes, Andrew Lovett et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Viewers first segment a chart into units and then compare them. Visual grouping determines which comparisons, and therefore which conclusions, come first.

title: The Arrangement of Marks Impacts Afforded Messages: Ordering, Partitioning, Spacing, and Coloring in Bar Charts
authors: Racquel Fygenson, Steven Franconeri, Enrico Bertini
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Ordering, partitioning, spacing and coloring of bars systematically shift which message (ranking, grouping, part-to-whole) viewers notice.

title: Declutter and Focus: Empirically Evaluating Design Guidelines for Effective Data Communication
authors: Kiran Ajani, Elsie Lee-Robbins, Cindy Xiong et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Evidence for Knaflic-style guidelines. Decluttering raised ratings of professionalism. Adding focus (headline, highlight color, annotation) raised aesthetics and clarity ratings and improved memory for the highlighted pattern.

title: Designing With Pictographs: Envision Topics Without Sacrificing Understanding
authors: Alyxander Burns, Cindy Xiong, Steven Franconeri et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Pictograph arrays vs bar and pie charts showed no overall difference in accuracy for extracting information or generating insights. Preferences were split.

title: The Role of Text in Visualizations: How Annotations Shape Perceptions of Bias and Influence Predictions
authors: Chase Stokes, Cindy Xiong, Marti A. Hearst
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Adding text barely changed predictions of data trends but strongly changed how biased the author was perceived to be. More biased wording led to more perceived bias.

title: Do You See What I See? A Qualitative Study Eliciting High-Level Visualization Comprehension
authors: Ghulam Jilani Quadri, Arran Zeyu Wang, Zhehao Wang et al.
venue: ACM CHI 2024
finding: The statistics people estimate accurately in perception studies differ from the patterns they naturally take away from line, bar and scatter charts.

title: In Pursuit of Error: A Survey of Uncertainty Visualization Evaluation
authors: Jessica R. Hullman, Xiao Li Qiao, Michael Correll et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Taxonomy of uncertainty-visualization evaluation applied to 86 studies. Most studies over-rely on performance and satisfaction measures.

title: Uncertainty Displays Using Quantile Dotplots or CDFs Improve Transit Decision-Making
authors: Michael Fernandes, Logan Walls, Sean A. Munson et al.
venue: ACM CHI 2018
finding: Quantile dotplots (50 dots) led to decisions at 97% of optimal payoff, 5 pp above no-uncertainty displays, and more consistent ones (within-subject SD 3 vs 7 pp). CDFs came close; text uncertainty was worse.

title: When (ish) is My Bus?
authors: Matthew Kay, Tara Kola, Jessica R. Hullman et al.
venue: Proceedings of the 2016 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Quantile dotplots reduced the variance of probability estimates about 1.15× compared to density plots on small screens and increased confidence.

title: Decision making with visualizations: a cognitive framework across disciplines
authors: Lace Padilla, Sarah H. Creem-Regehr, Mary Hegarty et al.
venue: Cognitive Research Principles and Implications
finding: Dual-process framework for decisions with visualizations: fast, heuristic Type 1 vs slow, effortful Type 2. Draws on empirical studies across disciplines.

title: Effects of ensemble and summary displays on interpretations of geospatial uncertainty data
authors: Lace Padilla, Ian T. Ruginski, Sarah H. Creem-Regehr
venue: Cognitive Research Principles and Implications
finding: The hurricane 'cone of uncertainty' (a summary display) is misread as storm size. Ensemble track displays led to more accurate interpretations.

title: How Visualizing Inferential Uncertainty Can Mislead Readers About Treatment Effects in Scientific Results
authors: Jake M. Hofman, Daniel G. Goldstein, Jessica R. Hullman
venue: ACM CHI 2020
finding: With 95% confidence intervals instead of prediction intervals, people paid more for and overestimated treatment effects. Prediction intervals and HOPs reduced the error.

title: Visual Reasoning Strategies for Effect Size Judgments and Decisions
authors: Alex M. Kale, Matthew J. Kay, Jessica R. Hullman
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Adding means to uncertainty displays slightly biases people toward ignoring uncertainty. The best design for estimating effect size is not the best for decisions, and users satisfice with heuristics.

title: A Task-Based Taxonomy of Cognitive Biases for Information Visualization
authors: Evanthia Dimara, Steven Franconeri, Catherine Plaisant et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Task-based taxonomy of 154 cognitive biases relevant to visualization, in 7 categories.

title: The Attraction Effect in Information Visualization
authors: Evanthia Dimara, Anastasia Bezerianos, Pierre Dragicevic
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: The decoy (attraction) effect appears in scatterplots and persists for larger sets of alternatives, which matters for dashboards used to choose options.

title: Pushing the (Visual) Narrative: The Effects of Prior Knowledge Elicitation in Provocative Topics
authors: Jeremy Heyer, Nirmal Kumar Raveendranath, Khairi Reda
venue: ACM CHI 2020
finding: Eliciting prior beliefs did not significantly change attitudes but increased surprise. Visualizations were more persuasive than equivalent text.

title: Explaining the Gap
authors: Yea-Seul Kim, Katharina Reinecke, Jessica Hullman
venue: Proceedings of the 2017 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Predict-then-see: participants who first predicted the data and explained the gap outperformed controls in recall and comprehension.

title: Data is Personal: Attitudes and Perceptions of Data Visualization in Rural Pennsylvania
authors: Evan M. Peck, Sofia E. Ayuso, Omar El-Etr
venue: ACM CHI 2019
finding: In rural Pennsylvania, education, political affiliation and personal experience shape attention to and trust in visualizations, and personal relevance drives engagement.

title: Dispersion Vs Disparity: Hiding Variability Can Encourage Stereotyping When Visualizing Social Outcomes
authors: Eli Holder, Cindy Xiong
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Charts that hide within-group variability (bars, dot plots) increased agreement with stereotyping explanations of group disparities. Jitter plots and prediction intervals reduced it.

title: Same Data, Diverging Perspectives: The Power of Visualizations to Elicit Competing Interpretations
authors: Cindy Xiong, Lisanne van Weelden, Adam G. Waytz et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Like ambiguous figures, the same data shown with different chart types or annotations split viewers' predictions depending on whether the historical lead or the momentum was salient.

title: Misleading Beyond Visual Tricks: How People Actually Lie with Charts
authors: Maxim Lisnic, Cole Polychronis, Alexander Lex et al.
venue: ACM CHI 2023
finding: Violations of design guidelines were not the main way people misled with charts. Reasoning errors built on faithfully plotted charts dominated.

title: Misinformed by Visualization: What Do We Learn From Misinformative Visualizations?
authors: Leo Yu‐Ho Lo, Ayush Gupta, Kento Shigyo et al.
venue: Computer Graphics Forum
finding: Taxonomy of 74 types of misleading issues found in real-world visualizations reported as misleading.

title: Illusion of Causality in Visualized Data
authors: Cindy Xiong, Joel Shapiro, Jessica R. Hullman et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Causal (mis)interpretation of correlations was highest for text and bar charts and weaker for scatterplots. Aggregating data into two groups increases perceived causality.

title: Graphs do not lead people to infer causation from correlation.
authors: Madison Fansher, Tyler James Adkins, Priti Pradhan Shah
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology Applied
finding: Adding graphs to news articles did not increase causal misinterpretation. The authors failed to replicate the claim that graphs make science more persuasive (Tal & Wansink, 2016).

title: The scale of COVID‐19 graphs affects understanding, attitudes, and policy preferences
authors: Alessandro Romano, Chiara Sotis, Goran Dominioni et al.
venue: Health Economics
finding: Log-scale COVID-19 death charts led to less accurate understanding and predictions and to different policy preferences than linear-scale charts.

title: Impact of COVID-19 forecast visualizations on pandemic risk perceptions
authors: Lace Padilla, Helia Hosseinpour, Racquel Fygenson et al.
venue: Scientific Reports
finding: Across 34 CDC visualizations of the same data, cumulative scales consistently raised perceived risk, and forecasts showing 6 or more models raised risk estimates more.

title: Swaying the Public? Impacts of Election Forecast Visualizations on Emotion, Trust, and Intention in the 2022 U.S. Midterms
authors: Fumeng Yang, Mandi Cai, Chloe Mortenson et al.
venue: OSF preprint
finding: Election forecast visualizations heightened emotion and trust and slightly affected intention to vote. Dual intervals had the strongest effects, and partisan gaps emerged.

title: Let’s Gamble: How a Poor Visualization Can Elicit Risky Behavior
authors: Melanie Bancilhon, Zhengliang Liu, Alvitta Ottley
venue: IEEE VIS 2020 (Short Papers)
finding: People gambled more when probabilities were shown with area-proportioned triangles and circles, so the encoding choice shifts risk behavior.

title: Improving Bayesian Reasoning: The Effects of Phrasing, Visualization, and Spatial Ability
authors: Alvitta Ottley, Evan M. Peck, Lane Harrison et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Bayesian-reasoning accuracy (6–62% in prior reports) rose to 77% with controlled text-plus-visualization designs, and up to 100% for people with high spatial ability.

title: Why Combining Text and Visualization Could Improve Bayesian Reasoning: A Cognitive Load Perspective
authors: Melanie Bancilhon, Amanda Jo Wright, Sunwoo Ha et al.
venue: ACM CHI 2023
finding: People with low working-memory capacity made fewer errors and felt less workload with icon arrays than with text alone.

title: My Model is Unfair, Do People Even Care? Visual Design Affects Trust and Perceived Bias in Machine Learning
authors: Aimen Gaba, Zhanna Kaufman, Jason Cheung et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Visual design shifts how people trade off fairness vs accuracy of ML models. Fairness weighed more when explained in text than in a bar chart, and women chose fairer models more often than men.

title: Trustworthy by Design: The Viewer's Perspective on Trust in Data Visualization
authors: Oen G. McKinley, Saugat Pandey, Alvitta Ottley
venue: ACM CHI 2025
finding: Viewers are consistent in their own trust rationale but disagree on which factors matter (clarity, data integrity, aesthetics, intent). Derives actionable guidelines for trustworthy design.

title: A Bayesian Cognition Approach to Improve Data Visualization
authors: Yea‐Seul Kim, Logan Walls, P. M. Krafft et al.
venue: ACM CHI 2019
finding: People update beliefs roughly like Bayesians for small samples but under-update for large-sample data, which gives a normative benchmark for evaluating visualizations.

title: From Perception to Decision: Assessing the Role of Chart Type Affordances in High-Level Decision Tasks
authors: Yixuan Li, Emery D. Berger, Minsuk Kahng et al.
venue: IEEE VIS 2025 (Short Papers)
finding: In a realistic decision (choosing a mentor), bar vs pie charts produced only minimal differences in outcomes. Perceptual advantages do not automatically carry over to high-level decisions.

title: Visualizing Uncertainty in Time Series Forecasts: The Impact of Uncertainty Visualization on Users' Confidence, Algorithmic Advice Utilization, and Forecasting Performance
authors: Dirk Leffrang, Oliver Müller
venue: Journal of Forecasting
finding: The relation between uncertainty visualization and forecasting performance is U-shaped. 95% prediction-interval plots helped most, compared with ensemble plots and point forecasts.

title: VLAT: Development of a Visualization Literacy Assessment Test
authors: Sukwon Lee, Sung-Hee Kim, Bum Chul Kwon
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: The VLAT has 53 items over 12 charts with reliability ω = 0.76. Literacy correlates r = 0.64 with learning an unfamiliar chart type.

title: Mini‐VLAT: A Short and Effective Measure of Visualization Literacy
authors: Saugat Pandey, Alvitta Ottley
venue: Computer Graphics Forum
finding: Mini-VLAT is a 12-item short form (ω = 0.72) that correlates strongly with the full VLAT. Practical for screening an audience.

title: CALVI: Critical Thinking Assessment for Literacy in Visualizations
authors: Lily W. Ge, Yuan Cui, Matthew J. Kay
venue: ACM CHI 2023
finding: CALVI is a 45-item test of how well people spot misleading design choices. The item bank is openly available.

title: Investigating aspects of data visualization literacy using 20 information visualizations and 273 science museum visitors
authors: Katy Börner, Adam Vincent Maltese, Russell N. Balliet et al.
venue: Information Visualization
finding: Most visitors could not name or interpret visualizations beyond basic charts, maps and graphs, almost none could read network layouts, and many relied on superficial features.

title: The Science of Visual Data Communication: What Works
authors: Steven Franconeri, Lace Padilla, Priti Pradhan Shah et al.
venue: Psychological Science in the Public Interest
finding: Research-based guidelines. The visual system extracts global statistics fast, but comparing subsets is slow. Good charts spare working memory, guide attention and respect conventions. Probably the best single entry point.

title: Visual Narrative Flow: Exploring Factors Shaping Data Visualization Story Reading Experiences
authors: Sean A. McKenna, Nathalie Henry Riche, Benjamin Lee et al.
venue: Computer Graphics Forum
finding: Visuals and navigation feedback (e.g. animated transitions) affected engagement with web data stories. The level of control (stepper vs continuous scroll) did not.

title: Linking and Layout: Exploring the Integration of Text and Visualization in Storytelling
authors: Qiyu Zhi, Alvitta Ottley, Ronald Metoyer
venue: Computer Graphics Forum
finding: Slideshow layouts beat vertical scrolling for comprehension. Linking text and chart interactively increased engagement and, in slideshows, recall.

title: The Curious Case of Combining Text and Visualization
authors: Alvitta Ottley, Aleksandra Kaszowska, R. Jordan Crouser et al.
venue: EuroVis 2019 (Short Papers)
finding: Visualizations make it easier to identify the critical information, but text makes it easier to extract once identified. People do not integrate well across the two.

title: Negative Emotions, Positive Outcomes? Exploring the Communication of Negativity in Serious Data Stories
authors: Xingyu Lan, Yanqiu Wu, Yang Shi et al.
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Evoking negative emotions in serious data stories fostered contemplation and long-term memory.

title: Smile or Scowl? Looking at Infographic Design Through the Affective Lens
authors: Xingyu Lan, Yang Shi, Yueyao Zhang et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Identified 12 affective responses to infographics and a taxonomy of design heuristics that trigger them.

title: Showing People Behind Data
authors: Jeremy Boy, Anshul Vikram Pandey, John Emerson et al.
venue: Proceedings of the 2017 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Anthropomorphized charts (showing the people behind the data) had very similar effects on empathy and donations as standard charts.

title: Can Anthropographics Promote Prosociality?A Review and Large-Sample Study
authors: Luiz Morais, Yvonne Jansen, Nazareno Andrade et al.
venue: Proceedings of the 2021 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: An information-rich anthropographic had at best a small effect on money allocation compared with a plain bar chart.

title: Comparing Effectiveness and Engagement of Data Comics and Infographics
authors: Zezhong Wang, Shunming Wang, Matteo Farinella et al.
venue: ACM CHI 2019
finding: Data comics were preferred for enjoyment and engagement and improved understanding and recall compared with infographics and illustrated text.

title: Hooked on data videos
authors: Fereshteh Amini, Nathalie Henry Riche, Bongshin Lee et al.
venue: Proceedings of the 2018 International Conference on Advanced Visual Interfaces
finding: Animation and pictographs in data videos each increased viewer engagement, on different engagement factors. Includes a validated engagement scale.

title: Dashboard Design Patterns
authors: Benjamin Bach, Euan Freeman, Alfie Abdul‐Rahman et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Eight groups of dashboard design patterns and dashboard genres (narrative, analytical, embedded), plus common design trade-offs.

title: What Do We Talk About When We Talk About Dashboards?
authors: Alper Sarikaya, Michael Correll, Lyn Bartram et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Design space of dashboards and major dashboard types. Shows dashboards are used far beyond monitoring (learning, communication).

title: Finding Their Data Voice: Practices and Challenges of Dashboard Users
authors: Melanie K. Tory, Lyn Bartram, Brittany Fiore-Gartland et al.
venue: IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications
finding: Dashboard users' engagement with data is intermittent and dependent on experts, and involves an awkward assembly of tools.

title: Untidy Data: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Tables
authors: Lyn Bartram, Michael Correll, Melanie K. Tory
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Business data workers use tables throughout sensemaking, not just for data cleaning, reshaping and marking up data directly. Tables are a visualization idiom in their own right.

title: The Unmet Data Visualization Needs of Decision Makers Within Organizations
authors: Evanthia Dimara, Harry Zhang, Melanie K. Tory et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Organizational decision makers need trade-off overviews, scenario analysis, interrogation tools and collaboration support, which analyst-oriented tools do not provide.

title: From Jam Session to Recital: Synchronous Communication and Collaboration Around Data in Organizations
authors: Matthew Brehmer, Robert Kosara
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Presenting data in organizations ranges from 'jam sessions' (team meetings) to 'recitals' (executive briefings). Progressive reveal is valued for directing attention.

title: Visualizing Ranges over Time on Mobile Phones: A Task-Based Crowdsourced Evaluation
authors: Matthew Brehmer, Bongshin Lee, Petra Isenberg et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: On phones, linear layouts of ranges over time were faster than radial ones with similar error rates.

title: Glanceable Visualization: Studies of Data Comparison Performance on Smartwatches
authors: Tanja Blascheck, Lonni Besançon, Anastasia Bezerianos et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: On smartwatches, simple comparisons took under 300 ms with bar charts and under 220 ms with donuts, but up to 1,780 ms with radial bars. Prefer bars or donuts for glanceable displays.

title: Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods
authors: William S. Cleveland, Robert McGill
venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association
finding: Origin of the channel ranking: position > length > angle/slope > area > volume > color. Recommends dot charts over pies and divided bars.

title: Crowdsourcing graphical perception
authors: Jeffrey Heer, Michael Bostock
venue: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Replicated Cleveland & McGill on Mechanical Turk and validated crowdsourcing for perception studies; also ranked area and other encodings.

title: What Makes a Visualization Memorable?
authors: Michelle A. Borkin, Azalea A. Vo, Zoya Bylinskii et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Memorability is consistent across people. Color, human-recognizable objects and visual density increase memorability, while common chart types are less memorable.

title: Useful junk?
authors: Scott Bateman, Regan L. Mandryk, Carl Gutwin et al.
venue: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Embellished 'chartjunk' charts were described no less accurately than plain ones and were recalled significantly better after 2–3 weeks.

title: Narrative Visualization: Telling Stories with Data
authors: Edward Segel, Jeffrey Heer
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Seven genres of narrative visualization and the spectrum from author-driven to reader-driven storytelling.

title: A Deeper Understanding of Sequence in Narrative Visualization
authors: Jessica R. Hullman, Steven M. Drucker, Nathalie Henry Riche et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Analysis of 42 professional slideshow-style narratives. Transition types between charts affect comprehension and preference, and consistent sequencing helps.

title: The Persuasive Power of Data Visualization
authors: Anshul Vikram Pandey, Anjali Manivannan, Oded Nov et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Charts were more persuasive than tables for people with weak or neutral initial attitudes. With strong opposing attitudes, tables persuaded better.

title: How Deceptive are Deceptive Visualizations?
authors: Anshul Vikram Pandey, Katharina Rall, Margaret L. Satterthwaite et al.
venue: Proceedings of the 33rd Annual ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Truncated axes, area as quantity, aspect-ratio tricks and inverted axes each significantly distorted the message viewers took away.

title: ISOTYPE Visualization
authors: Steve Haroz, Robert Kosara, Steven L. Franconeri
venue: Proceedings of the 33rd Annual ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Superfluous images distract, but pictographs that represent the data itself carry no cost and improve memory and engagement.

title: Storytelling in Information Visualizations
authors: Jeremy Boy, Francoise Detienne, Jean-Daniel Fekete
venue: Proceedings of the 33rd Annual ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Adding introductory 'stories' to exploratory visualizations did not increase user engagement in exploration.

title: Ranking Visualizations of Correlation Using Weber's Law
authors: Lane Harrison, Fumeng Yang, Steven Franconeri et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Precision of correlation judgments in 9 chart types follows Weber's law and differs strongly between positive and negative correlations.

title: Four Experiments on the Perception of Bar Charts
authors: Justin Talbot, Vidya Setlur, Anushka Anand
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Confirms Cleveland & McGill: stacked bars are much worse than aligned bars, and adjacent bars are compared more accurately than separated ones. Explains the sources of error.

title: An Evaluation of the Impact of Visual Embellishments in Bar Charts
authors: Drew Skau, Lane Harrison, Robert Kosara
venue: Computer Graphics Forum
finding: Some common bar-chart embellishments (e.g. rounded or triangular tops, extended bars) measurably reduce reading accuracy, while others are harmless.

title: Infographic Aesthetics
authors: Lane Harrison, Katharina Reinecke, Remco Chang
venue: Proceedings of the 33rd Annual ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: People form a reliable appeal judgment of an infographic within a mere-exposure glance. Age, gender and education shift preferred colorfulness and complexity.

title: Effectiveness of Animation in Trend Visualization
authors: George Croom Robertson, Roland Fernandez, Danyel Fisher et al.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
finding: Trend animation (Gapminder-style) is fast and enjoyable in presentations but error-prone. Small multiples are faster and more accurate for analysis.

title: Graph Literacy
authors: Mirta Galesic, Rocio Garcia-Retamero
venue: Medical Decision Making
finding: On average 9 of 13 graph-literacy items were correct in both countries, and about one third of adults have both low graph literacy and low numeracy.

title: Investigating Performance and Practices with Univariate Distribution Charts
authors: (see arXiv)
venue: arXiv preprint 2604.08378
finding: Boxplot vs violin vs histogram vs strip plot: preference and task performance systematically diverge. Boxplots are often misread for distribution shape, and strip plots perform surprisingly well for small datasets.
